speechtext: 12$ cents per hundred pounds?
That would be 37$ cents a barrel. Does the hon. minister think that taking the duty off would bring the price of cement down to what it was before the merger was formed?
There would still be a substantial reduction.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great at-

tention to the speech of my hon. Mend the Minister of Labour in moving the second reading of this measure. I am sure both the House and the country -will be surprised to know that the government, which came into power with the promise that they would abolish all those things that enhance the cost of living, has been 14 years in power, and this is the first real effort they have made to introduce legislation to cure these evils.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I am very glad to hear my hon. friend the Prime Minister say 'hear, hear' to that remark, because he was one of the chief movers in an agitation to educate the people of this country to the idea that protection was all wrong, and that when his party came into power it would abolish protection, and when that was done there would be no combines or mergers to affect the prices of goods to the people of Canada. Of course, this is ancient history, and I am inclined to apologize for introducing it on a question of so much importance as the present question. But I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that it was not the present government that made the first effort in Canada to cure these evils, but the late government, who in 1889, put upon the statute-book a law which I propose to take a few minutes of the time of the House to place before the House and the country. That legislation was introduced under the direction and guidance of . the late Hon. N. C. Wallace. It is chapter 4 of the statutes of 1889, and is as follows:
An Act for the Prevention and Suppression of Combinations formed in restraint of Trade.
(Assented to May 2, 1889.)
Whereas, it is expedient to declare the law *relating to conspiracies and combinations formed in restraint of trade and to provide penalties for the violation of the same: Therefore, Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, declares and enacts as follows:-[DOT]
1. Every person who conspires, combines, agrees or arranges with any other person, or with any railway, steamship or steamboat or transportation company, unlawfully-	. . .
(a)	To unduly limit the facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing or dealing in any article or commodity which may be a subject of trade or commerce; or
(b)	To restrain or injure trade or commerce in relation to any such article or commodity, or to unreasonably enhance the price thereof; or
(c)	To unduly prevent, limit, or lessen the manufacture or production of any such

article or commodity, or to unreasonably enhance the price thereof; or
(d)	To unduly prevent or lessen competition in the production, manufacture, purchase, barter, sale, transportation or supply of any such article or commodity, or in the price of insurance * upon person or property-
Is guilty of a misdemeanour and liable, on conviction, to a penalty not exceeding four thousand dollars and not less than two hundred dollars, or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding two years; and, if a corporation, is liable, on conviction, to a penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars and not less than one thousand dollars.
This is the first and only law to be found on the statute-book of Canada which aims to deal with combines and mergers. It is fair to say that subsequently a clause was inserted in the tariff legislation of 1897 by this government, that aimed to cure these evils, and after that a Bill was introduced by the Minister of Inland Revenue, now the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, dealing with a similar matter. But, I am quite correct . in saying that the legislation placed upon the statute-book by the administration of 1889-is the only special legislation aimed at dealing with this important, question. .

It was in 1897, the year after this government came to power, that the government passed the first legislation dealing with this matter. When the hon. gentleman said it was in 1907, no doubt he doubt he made a slip.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman whether the legislation he has just read added anything to the existing legislation on this matter at that time? Was it not merely declaratory of the common law as it then was?

in the past. I do not offer any special criticism to the department of the hon. minister, but I do not think it requires a special commission to discover evils which are plain to the eye of every man. It is quite within the competency of the Department of Labour to find out, with its present organization, wdiether prices are higher than they should be, and having found that out to correct the evils with the power already at hand. No doubt the Bill makes it easier for the public to institute proceedings to discover whether or not these evils exist, and it proposes that the government shall pay the costs of any trial of the kind whether the charges are true or untrue. That is helpful, and I have no opposition to offer to it. We on this side of the House wall assist in every possible way in that respect. But what the people of Canada are looking for is not new legislation, but enforcement of the existing legislation, and what is the complaint against this government and against the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is none.

Oh, yes, there are many complaints, but ~ my right hon. friend turns a deaf ear to them. The charge against this government and against the Department of Labour is, that the government does not put in force the laws already upon the statute-books in respect to combines and in respect to many other matters. Instead of the government striking at these evils with the ample machinery at present under their control, they'are simply introducing a new remedy so as to lead the people of Canada to think that they are doing something for them. If the Minister of Labour had been able to come to this House and to state that he had investigated these evils and found they did exist in Canada, and that the government had put into force the legislation now at their command with a view to crushing these evils, he would have received the commendation of the people of the country, but, he has chosen to place another law on the statute-book which he asks the people to enforce, and not the government whose duty it is to enforce these laws.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The hon. gentleman from Peel (Mr. Blain) has not grasped the intent of this legislation. I take issue with him when he says that the legislation now on the statute-books might well be used to carry out the purpose of this Bill as framed. Looking at the legislation now in existence, it appears to me most distinctly that the machinery provided is absolutely not ample to give effect to the provisions of this Bill. If it were, I would agree with the hon. gentleman that we should not enact any more legislation than is necessary.
Is it intended that chap. 41 of 52 Victoria shall be repealed by this Act ?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I should suppose not.
If it is not, you will readily see that the right of every Crown prosecutor throughout the provinces would still exist on an information sworn.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
That might be, but if the machinery provided in this Act is better than that provided in any other Act, surely it would be taken advantage of. Now, Mr. Speaker, after the extremely able and comprehensive speech by the Minister of Labour any further argument in favour of the Bill would be mere surplusage. I Tose to say that I am heartily in favour of the Bill submitted by the hon. gentleman. .There can be no doubt that there are combines and combines. In the old days we had the Farmers' Alliance, which started stores and gave to those in the membership of the Alliance cheaper goods than they had been hitherto getting, and we had also the organization of the Grain Growers of the West, the efforts of which were directed towards a similar end. These combines were certainly beneficial in their effects. But there are other combines which have an evil effect on the community, and it is at such that this Bill is aimed. There is a decided conviction in the public mind that whether or not it is merely a coincidence, the price of food and the price of the necessities of life are going up by leaps and bounds contemporaneously with the organization of these combines. The people of Canada are asking that the facts should be investigated and that machinery for that purpose should be provided by the government. The very title of the Bill gives its intent; it is an Act ' to provide for the investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts, and mergers which may enhance prices or restrict competition to the detriment of consumers.' The hon. member for Lanark told us that he did not think it possible that any commission could find out what did or did not enhance prices, but I hardly think the hon. gentleman was correct in that. Do we not know as a matter of fact that it is a systematized plan of the manufacturers that in many cases they do sell goods cheaper to the foreigner than they do to the home market? As I understand it, protection was put on for the sake of fostering industries in the Dominion of Canada and encouraging competition, but it certainly never was the intention that protection should enable these manufacturers to combine together and enhance the price of commodities to the consumers.
If, therefore, as I think there can be any doubt it will be shown and can be shown that foreigners receive goods cheaper than the home market, surely there is an en-

hancement of price to the home consumer. If that is so, it will be only dealing justly with the people of Canada that that should be taken cognizance of and1 that machinery should be provided to overcome that condition. There is no doubt that sugar, groceries, glassware, harness and similar staple goods are subject, if not to a combine, at least to sale at set prices laid down by a combination of manufacturers. The everyday consumer, farmer or other has to pay that. There is ample evidence of this, as can be shown by circulars of manufacturers, merchants and others. If that is so, the very first object of this Bill has been accomplished when it can be shown by evidence taken before one of these commissions that such prices are being charged by reason of the combine and the power of the commission to see that the goods are sold to the consumer at a fair price and at a reasonable profit.' It is the duty of this parliament and of all legislatures to legislate in that way. We are here to legislate for the common good. We know that these abuses are committed every day. We know as a matter of fact, that in Toronto alone, there is one concern that makes thousands of dollars a year simply by collecting rebates and discounts from the jobbers by reason of the combines agreeing to sell only to them. Surely this should be remedied by this parliament at the first opportunity. I say that simply because the farmer, by reason of the enhanced prices, and not because of any combination on his part, but simply by reason of the ordinary law of supply and demand, is now receiving good rates for his produce, and goodness knows the farmer deserves to do well, because for many years he barely made a living and had hard work at that, it is not right to say that he can go on paying for the commodities that he uses at these enhanced prices. I say that he and every other consumer has a right to be protected by this parliament and, therefore, I think this legislation is absolutely necessary.

My hon. friend and others have been talking in reference to the Bill. As I understand, we have no Bill before us, but simply a resolution, and it might be better to pass the resolution and have the discussion on the Bill itself. I Understood it w^as the wish of the Prime Minister that we should have this session close by the first of May. I do not see how he can intend that when his minister in introducing this Bill has spent three and a half hours.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well spent, even if we prorogue on the second of May.

Is it the intention of the Prime Minister as soon as the resolution passes, to take up the Bill and then have the discussion in committee?
Mr. PARDEE

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

This Bill, to my mind, savours a good deal of class legislation, and we should be very careful how we deal with this matter. It has been brought into the House by the Minister of Labour, I believe largely for the purpose of meeting the reflex echo of a tremendous muck-raking campaign that has been carried on in the United States against the so-called trusts and combines. I have heard many members of the House to-day state that there are combines and trusts in this country. I challenge any one of those members who have made that statement to name a combine in this country, not a merger, a combine. You see there is absolute silence, there is not a member here who can of his own knowledge say there is an actual combine. That shows this legislation is largely the outcome of newspaper bunkum, and my hon. friend the Minister of Labour is the most assiduous reader of newspaper and publicity in the House. There are combines and mergers, and the distinction must not be overlooked. I have a great deal of respect for the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark), because he goes to the bottom of ail questions, argues them from the beginning and takes a reasonable view. When the government place, a protective tariff around the country and place the men with blue coats and brass buttons around the barriers, there is no question that that forms a trust. After a while when we have practically established industries in the country and they find that they are cutting into each other's prices, there has been in the past a tendency to form what are called combines. A combine is formed when half a dozen manufacturers of an article, or all the manufacturers of an article in the country, meet together and fix the price. They can do that to-day and can evade the Criminal Code and1 this Act and everything else. As a matter of fact, there have been prosecutions-I was going to say persecutions, because these criminal prosecutions have really resulted in destroying the health and the mentality of good men in this country, these prosecutions of men simply because three or four of them get together and say: We cannot afford to -sell except at a certain price, and agree to that and1 fix the price. For this they were placed in the criminal dock. In the United States they have had similar prosecutions. But to-day there is a changed condition of affairs brought about by these prosecutions. What is that changed condition of affairs? They have accentuated this thing and made it worse still, they have brought about the merger. Men take advantage of the joint stock companies law, they issue stock in a company embracing all their factories, and

in that way there is only one company in the country carrying on business, just as the hon. member has mentioned in the case of the cement merger. Let us get down to business and see whether we are doing justice to all parties concerned.
Do these prosecutions take place under the Criminal Code?

I have had no experience, but I know they have been conducted. A number of our leading men have been brought into the criminal court, and their cases have been held for months and almost years, they have been penalized by expensive lawyers, and one or two of those attacks on so-called combinations have not beeq finished yet.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that it is under the law to which the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) has made reference that all these prosecutions have taken place?

I grant that that law should be changed in some respects because I do not think it is fair that these people should be prosecuted when another branch of labour is. allowed to go free. Now let me see. You would take in the manufacturing business, and the manufacturing business seems to be the one that is going to be subject to the . imposition. Every one seems to have his harpoon in the manufacturer. When the interests of the manufacturer suffer the interests of the labourer suffer; because if you close up the factories of this country and throw down the tariff walls, as is proposed to be done in some of your legislation, what happens? You are escaping from one small trust to get under the heel of a greater trust, because that is what will occur. If you throw down the tariff wall between this country and the United States, are you going into a country where everything is free, where labour is free, and there are no trusts? No, Sir, you are immediately placing the industry of this country under the heel of a greater trust. The hon. member for Lambton sits for a riding where the greatest trust of this country has its headquarters, and that is the Standard Oil Trust. If you conduct business in that way you are going to throw this country absolutely under the control, not of a national trust, but of an international trust.
Now let us follow this thing logically. There are three interests concerned in this attack. One is"capital. We have no sympathy with capital, of course, because the newspapers, and all the novelists and everybody who writes about everything are down on capital. But capital is very necessary sometimes when there are hard times,
or when you want to buy a meal. The interest of capital is altogether forgotten in this Bill. Another interest is that of labour. Now what happens to labour? I believe that labour ought to be protected to a certain extent, and that capital should be protected to the same extent. As it is to-day, the manufacturer finds himself up against these conditions. He finds that his men all combine, and form a labour union, and they say: We won't sell our labour to you except at such a figure. I have scanned this Bill, and I must tell the Minister of Labour that after reading the provisions of this Bill it seems to me that the machinery of this Bill can be brought against a labour union, it will be brought under the action of this Bill just the same as any other institution, there is no protection for them. But the tendency of the law in his department has been to say to the labourer, who forms only one element in the community :	We will protect you in seeing that
you may not sell your labour except at a certain figure. But after the manufacturer has put his capital into this business, after he has bought his raw material, and put his machines to work, after he has finished that stuff, if he tries to protect himself in any way, or joins another manufacturer, and they say: We cannot sell this stuff except at a certain figure, having regard to what it has cost us, then those manufacturers are proceeded against. I believe the only correct way to deal with this question is to deal with it from the . broad standpoint of the common law. As the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) says, let there be absolute freedom in these matters. The more you institute class legislation, the more you are setting class against class, because when you start to protect the interest of one class you are injuring the interest of another class.
This Bill proposes to deal with combines. What are combines for? Combines are for the purpose, not of enhancing prices-the Minister of Labour is so far off the mark that he does not know what he is talking about when he makes a Bill of that kind. The first object of a combination is to eliminate competition. If there is freedom of competition, the hon. member for Red Deer will tell you, prices will be at the normal and proper value. In order to enhance prices you must eliminate competition, is that not so? Does this Bill deal with the elimination of competition? No, it proposes ostensibly to deal with enhanced prices. Now. let us get down to the prices. The hon. minister stated that the board would go to work and ascertain the cost, and the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McLean) said that the cost of these things will be got at. If either one of these gentlemen are capable of getting at the

cost of anything, there are lots of big institutions in this country that will give them $10,000 a year if they will tell what actual costs are going to be. There is a branch in every successful enterprise that does nothing else but keep track of the costs. The cost to-day will be a certain figure on a certain article; to-morrow, even so small a thing as the humidity of the atmosphere changes the cost in a great many cases. You will be surprised to know that there are so many conditions constantly changing that you cannot get at the real cost of an article; so he is travelling very far afield.
Again I say that this legislation is of a vicious character. Why, it would have been well for us to have halted and not have gone on with any of this muck-raking legislation this session, because the United States papers that I have read, the financial papers, have been pointing to Canada as a country of level-headed business men, as a country where capital is to receive a certain measure of protection. Now, they claim there is no protection to capital in England, which country is sending it over here by the wheelbarrow load, and in the United States they are prosecuting capitalists, and the capitalists of the United States are beginning to say: Well, Canada is going to be a great country in the future, the legislatures of Canada have great respect for capital. For that reason, I say that it is extremely unfortunate that we should introduce into this House, at this period, legislation of that kind, legislation that can be by any means construed as an attack on capital. I regret very much to hear the remarks made by some hon. members here to-day who take class views of this matter. I am just as much opposed to combinations as any man. I could name you one or two combines which are to-day forming mergers or trusts, and there is no law that can be passed in this House that will reach them. Once a great big merger is formed in the manufacture of any article, that moment competition ceases, because no one will venture his capital into that line in opposition to trust.
There is another feature of this legislation that I think this House should consider very seriously. There is no question that at the bottom of all those social questions-for this is after all a social question-there is springing up various ideas of a socialistic character, opposition to one class or opposition to another. The greatest interest possibly in this country to-day is the commercial interest; because when a man speaks of his riding, when he speaks of the growth of the country, when he speaks of the growth of his city, he means its commercial greatness, does he not?

Now, the one interest that is not represented by a committee of this House whereby it may be protected, the one interest that is not represented here by a minister with a committee behind his back, is the commercial interest and manufacturing interest of this country. I hope that this House will take that question seriously into consideration. Why should these great interests be subject to penalization constantly? Why should not the manufacturing and trading interests of the country .be represented in this House just as well as the labour interest? I do not deny my good friends on the side of labour for one moment their right to be heard here, or elsewhere. I have always listened with a great deal of admiration and respect to those men who represent labour. They are not hypocrites. They know what they want, and they rise and speak their own minds here. But, when it comes to a question of the manufacturers it is different. The manufacturers are essential, because if you close up the large manufactories the labourers of this country -would suffer, they would have to close their homes and go to foreign countries, where the articles are manufactured that should be manufactured in Canada.
Who will buy from the manufacturers?

Nobody, for the simple reason that the moment that you make it impossible for the manufacturer to manufacture he must close his door. I know something about cement which is spoken of here. What was the matter with cement? Competition had reached such a keen state that the manufacturers of cement were actually selling it at from fifteen to twenty-eight cents a barrel less than it cost them. What brought this about? There is, in the United States, a great big cement trust whose headquarters are in the Alleghany and Lehigh valleys. That company came to this country, established a branch and said to the manufacturers : We are going to drive you out of business or you will have to come into the trust with us. At the time cement was selling $1.50 a barrel but in the face of that they sold their cement for 95 cents and forced the Canadian companies to form a merger of which they are the largest part and which they now control. That is how you have got your price up to $1.50 a barrel to-day. If the manufacturers in Canada are not to have freedom of contract there is not a line of manufacturing but what, in three or four years, will be forced to go into these mergers or forced out of business by the American trusts, and there will be nothing that will not be

controlled by foreign tru'sts with enormous capital. I trust that this House will send this Bill to a committee. I realize that there are interests at stake, such as those of the consumer, which should be recognized. I realize that it is a great wrong that manufacturers, or any other class of the community, should be allowed "to combine to the detriment of the public or to enhance prices, but at the same time, in looking at this question, we should look at it judicially and not take ' a one sided view of it because the question is too great a one for such treatment, and if we appoint a committee to take this Bill into consideration we should also consider the advisability of the establishment of a committee of this House on trade and commerce as we have a committee on public accounts and marine and fisheries. If this were done the labouring interests, the consumers and the manufacturers could come and tell their story to the members of this House and we would get at the actual facts and not be rushed into hasty legislation through a lot of mere newspaper talk. My hon. friend from Bed Deer (Mr. Clark) is a great free trader but, if before that committtee he found that anything was going to injure this country I am satisfied that he would stand shoulder to shoulder with any man here in advocating that which was in the best interests of the country. I am one of the protectionists, so-called, of this House, but while that is so, if it were shown to me that our country was going to be benefited by free trade I would be willing to foreswear my allegiance with the protective party and join his ranks. We have no means of hearing the arguments of those interested at the bar of this House, or before any committee, and I hope this Bill will be threshed out well in committee and a hearing given to all interests concerned. If that is done I do not think this Bill will emerge in the form in which the Minister of Labour has put it. I know he is a young man and enthusiastic upon these things, but I think he is too much inclined to look upon them through spectacles that only give him one vision of the conditions with which he is attempting to deal. We remember the old story about the two parties in Borne that quarrelled, and when one took the opposite side to the other and threatened to start another city they were told that one part of the body could not get along without the other. It is the same here; the interests of the manufacturer, the labourer and the consumer are so closely interlaced and identified that we cannot do justice to the country unless we consider them all.

sider the resolutions in connection with Bill (No. 101) respecting the investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers.

Mr. Speaker, when the minister first introduced the Bill respecting combines he asked for the support of the House, and I frankly told him that if it commended itself to my judgment it would certainly have my support. I agreed with him that some authority was needed to control combines, trusts and .mergers. Since then I have examined the Bill somewhat cursorily, and I must confess that I was surprised and disappointed that it simply is a measure providing for inquiry and report. The minister told us that he depended more upon publicity to cure the evil than upon penal legislation, and in pursuance of that idea he has provided no penalties in this Bill for infringement i Act. The hon. gentleman told us also that the Combines Bill of 1889 failed of its purpose though the penalties under it were severe, but let us inquire why that Act was a failure. We were given the opinion of the late Sir Oliver Mowat, who, when asked to punish those who were acting in violation of that law, stated that although the attorney general of each province was charged with the responsibility, no attorney general could hope to successfully enforce it He said it was impossible to go into court and prove what was unduly or unreasonably enhancing the value. It was the verv wording of the law which made it useless and worse than a waste of time to attempt to enforce it. Now, how came that law to be enacted in that way? It was not the late Hon. N. Clarke Wallace who introduced it in that form at all. It w'as amended in that way in the Senate. I was there and assisted Mr. Wallace as best I could
w g6u- t}le Bil1 tllr<)ugh the Senate as it left this House, but we were unable to prevail on the members of that honourable body to put it through as it left this House. They amended it by introducing the words ''unduly' and 'unreasonably' in it, making it so that it was of little value thereafter. That was the cause of the failure of the law, and not because it imposed a penalty for the violation of the law. We appealed to the federal parliament to enforce the law, but they said it was not the duty of the federal parliament to enforce any law, but the duty of the province. When we appealed to Sir Oliver Mowat, he gave the reason I have stated why the law could not be enforced. Therefore it was not enforced, and was not effective. But the hon. member said what was true, that the evidence taken before the commission of inquiry, and the facts disclosed to the world had such an effect that a number of combines ceased to operate, because of the pub-Mr. GRAHAM.
licity. Some of them did not, and to that extent it did good, but it did not go as far as it ought to have gone. Who is responsible, I ask, for that law having been a failure? I say the present government are responsible. In 1899 I introduced a Bill for the purpose of amending section 520 of the Criminal Code by striking out the words 'unduly' and 'unreasonably.' I got that Bill through this House one session, but it was thrown out by the Senate. I got it through both House the next session. But who amended that law? It was the present government, by the then Minister of Justice, new Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. He slipped through an amendment to section 520, of the Criminal Code, restoring those objectionable words, and it passed this House without my knowing it. When the Bill to amend the Criminal Code was before the House, I asked for an explanation, and the hon. member was cute enough to explain several clauses of the Bill, but refrained from saying one word as to this; and, not being a lawyer, I did not pay as much attention to the Bill as I ought to have done. From that day to this no attempt has been made to enforce the law, and if it is a failure the present government are absolutely and unequivocably responsible.

In addition to the words ' unduly ' and ' unreasonably,' was not the word ' unlawfully ' also in the Bill as it first passed this House, and I think the word ' unlawfully ' was stricken out in the Senate, and the words ' unduly ' and ' unreasonably ' left in,

The word unlawfully was never called in question, so far as I know. That was not what affected the law. It was the words ' unduly ' and ' unreasonably.' If the law was a failure, the present government were certainly responsible for it. The present government deluded the country for a length of time by saying that they had made a better provision in the law. They inserted a provision in the Tariff Act saying that where it was established to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council that there was a combination in restraint of trade upon any article imported into this country upon which there was a duty, the Governor in Council might admit the article free of duty or so reduce the duty thereon as to give the public the benefit of reasonable competition in the article if it appeared to the Governor in Council that such disadvantage to the consumer was facilitated by the duties imposed on the article. Now, I brought to the attention of this House the grievance of those parties who were affected by the leather combine,

and read their affidavits made under oath. It was proven up to the hilt, in a very elaborate case, prepared by Mr. Garrow, before he was appointed to the bench, that the combine gave a rebate of 5 per cent to certain firms who handled certain kinds of leather, and thereby made it impossible for those who would not agree to buy from them to carry on business as they had done previously.
Right in my own village there was a tannery that was making certain kinds of leather. The tannery was unable to sell in Toronto to the firm it used to deal with on account of this combine.. I have letter after letter from men in the tanning business in exactly the same position. They could not sell the leather because they refused to enter into this combine. I had the arrangements that were made and declarations by a large number of eminent men in that line, creditable witnesses, who were prepared to prove the combine was a nefarious one, but although I called upon the government to act, they refused.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look into the case, he will find that action under the tariff law would not have granted the relief he desired. If the duty had been taken off leather altogether, the very, small tanner, in whose interests my hon. friend was pleading, would have been affected. That was a case vdiich did not come within the tariff law.

The hon. minister is mistaken. What these men requested was that the duty should be taken off the kinds of leather in which this combine was principally dealing, such as Spanish soles, and which were not tanned in the small tanneries. But why could not this agreement have been attacked under the Criminal Code, had the government desired to break up this combine, or under the customs law which they professed to have made for that purpose. But they did absolutely nothing. Mr. Smith, of Chatham, told me that Beardmore and Company of Halton, Mr. Charlie Hyman, of London, Mr. Davis, of Newmarket, were in the combine and, as these were friends and supporters of the government, the government refused to act. I was, therefore, justified in making the statement 1 did this afternoon, and which I did in 1907, namely that the goverilment would not be likely to act against any combines in which their friends were interested. Experience has justified the forecast I then made. If the present Bill were to be effective, I would gladly welcome it, but I am inclined to think it will not. Why? Because there is no penalty. What is publicity? The weakest feature of the Rail-219
way Commission in the United States today is that they depended on publicity; but they found that, when they came to put the Act in force, it was comparatively a failure. Some say that its failure was due to state rights, but I met one of their own men who reviewed the subject very carefully and intelligently, and he said that the weakest feature of their Act was the lack of power to enforce it, and inflict a penalty for violation of it.

Possibly my hon. friend has not read the penaltv clauses of this measure. The difficulty in connection with the alleged leather combine which he mentions, he says, was that he could not- get the government to move and ascertain whether such a combine existed or not. But under this Bill any individual can start the machinery for investigation; and if the investigation shows that a combine exists, the Governor in Council has power to remove or lower the tariff on the finding of one of these boards. .
What clause gives that power? You have repealed section 12 of the Customs Act of 1907, which deals with it.

Section 21 provides for the removal or reduction of customs duties in order to secure reasonable competition. The clause repealed of the Tariff Act of 1907, is carried over into this Bill with the additional provision that the finding of a board constituted under this measure, may 'be a sufficient warrant to the Governor in Council to take action, and similarly as respects the Inland Revenue Act, if it is shown by one of the boards that a combine exists among dealers with regard to goods, for the sale of which they must obtain a license from the Department of Inland Revenue, a clause in that Act would permit the Governor in Council to cancel the_ license. A similar cause exists in this Bill with regard to cases in which it is shown that the holders of patents are taking advantage of them to the prejudice of the public. In addition to these penalties, if it is found that, the parties are guilty of a course of action detrimental to consumers, and against the interests of the public the parties so reported against do not comply within ten davs in making the change desired, they are liable to a specific penalty provided in this Bill.
Where is that penalty?
That is section 23 which imposes a penalty of a general nature on com-
bines, restricting manufacture or competition, my hon. friend could hardly have noticed this section.

I went through the Bill hurriedly and did not notice it, and of course that section is an improvement. There, are many articles which are the subject of combine and in regards to which the changing of the customs duty would not be an effective remedy. Unless we are able to attack these combines under the Criminal Code or unless some other penalty be imposed, the Act would only be partially successful.
Quite so.

That would make it a great deal better in my judgment and give it some value, but I do hold the opinion very strongly that while publicity may sometimes prevent the doing of improper things, it does not go far enough. With reference to the Labour Act, which we passed, to my mind, that was its defect. No doubt the hon. minister will contend that that Act has been very valuable.
Hear, hear.
It has been of some value, but if there had been put into that Act a compulsory arbitration clause, it would be much more valuable. That is what the Australians think.
I do not think their Act has proved as effective as ours.

I think it has proved comparatively successful. I have followed up its workings and the Australians give it credit for doing a great deal of good. Take our Railway Commission. The first proposal was to establish it on the same lines as the United States Railway Commission, but that was proved a failure because it has no power to order and compel the doing of certain things under a severe penalty, sp we clothed our Railway Commissioners with authority to compel that to be done which they ordered. Therefore, ours has proved much more effective and valuable. The defect in this Bill would be in my judgment where we did not take
power and authority, over and above publicity to enforce our ruling and the right given to individuals to put the law in action whether the government be willing or not is a move in the right direction. But over and above all that what is required is an effective penalty that will compel combines to observe the law and punish those who violate it.

I am very pleased to
think that the government have at last taken up this matter. I think this is the first practical step they have taken in the thirteen years they have held office as an attempt to deal with what is considered a very serious problem. The idea prevails pretty generally that the. consuming public of this country are being taxed unduly by what are generally termed combines. Whether that prevails to the extent the general public believe or not, I am not prepared to say, but I do believe there are instances where combinations to unduly enhance prices do prevail. The impression prevails in some quarters that this can be cured by a change in the tariff. I do not myself believe that very much can be done in that direction. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) attempted to deal with that aspect of the case and left the impression on those who had not considered the matter very carefully that the whole trouble arose from our having what is termed a protective or revenue tariff, and I think he left the impression on the House that it was only in countries like Canada and the United States, which have protective tariffs, that combines can grow and flourish, and he gave us an instance of an attempt to form a combine in Great Britain by the Lever'Soap Company, stating that the people had boycotted that firm and had succeeded in breaking up the combine. He did not tell us the reason why the people objected to the combine . The reason was that they had been bitten by other combines in Great Britain. There are innumerable smaller combines dealing in almost every known article used in Great Britain. Now I do not think that by changing our tariff it will meet the difficulty that presents itself. The question that, presents itself to my mind is just how far the minister would go in the application of his measure. In dealing with matters of trade there are so many things that at once arise, many small considerations that might not seem large in themselves, but
where a principle is at stake. We will suppose that in a village or town the barbers get together and say: We cannot cut hair at the same price as we did before, and they form a combination to keep the prices up to a certain figure, and they give notice that after such a period they will charge a certain price to customers. This runs through the shoemakers, the blacksmiths, the carpenters, and through all the trades with which the people are dealing. Would the minister, in the application of this measure, attempt to deal with all these small matters? If he attempts to do that, it seems to me he will be trying to deal with a very large problem indeed.

I understand the hon. gentleman is asking me a question. Several points have been raised in the nature of questions such as the hon. gentleman has just put, and I think it would be more convenient to answer them in committee. If hon. members will adopt the resolution and pass the second reading of the Bill and get at once into committee, then I could answer all these questions and save a good deal of time.

I am willing to leave these matters for the minister to answer them in committee. I may say that so far as I am concerned I believe that the minister is moving along the right line. He seems determined to grapple with this question in a vigorous way, and for that I commend him. I think he is moving in the right direction. I believe that all combines have the effect of enhancing prices to the consumer. I do not care whether the combines are entered into in Great Britain, or in Canada, or in the United States. I do not care what kind of trade policy a country may have, when these combines are brought into play they have the effect of lessening competition, and when you lessen competition I think the natural outcome is an increase in price. Suppose three or four storekeepers get together and make a combine and agree to operate under one management, that eliminates competition, and the result is a general increase of price. I do not suppose that all the combines that are entered into have the object of raising prices. There are many other factors that move men to form combines. I think one chief reason is to do away with a great deal of expense, and there are many other reasons why it is more profitable for several firms to come under one management. But the result generally is that the people will pay a little more for the article than they would pay otherwise. People are complaining a great deal now of the cost of living, particularly of the cost of food stuffs.
Now a great cause of the increase of prices is the failure of supply to meet the demand. Some people aTgue that by jree trade you would diminish the cost of living. Supposing you took down the bars altogether, it would not make much difference. The people have to live on the produce of the farms, and I do not believe that the farmers are getting higher prices than they are entitled to. But I Jo think something might be done in the way of lessening the cost between the original producer and the consumer, and that is one of the reasons why I advocate a home market, and the bringing of the consumer and the producer together. That will provide a home market for the farmers of this country. But that is not what is aimed at undetf this Bill, this is not the occasion, I suppose, to discuss that ques-Mr. WRIGHT.
tion. I simply rose to say that this is something that will have to be grappled with. The combines and the effect of combines are something the government will have to take hold of and deal with in a drastic manner. It will not do to put some little Bill upon the statute-book and leave it there, and let things drift along. We will have to take hold of the problem in a way that will touch any firms that get together and form a conspiracy-to increase prices where there is actually a conspiracy it comes under the Criminal Code. A weak point in the Bill, to my mind, is that there is no proper method of getting hold of that evil. Another very serious difficulty is that of arriving at the value of articles. I do not think that, unless soiite tribunal is arranged for, that the minister can make his Bill effective, and that it will satisfy the general public, people that are charged with making a combine and people that are affected by a combine, some tribunal to wdiich both sides can appeal with confidence. Without such a tribunal I do not see how you are going to get at the facts as to whether a price has been unduly increased or not. I do not see how the board that the minister purposes introducing will deal with that effectively. He is going to appoint two men to that board, and they will be required to investigate the facts. In the processes of manufacture there are a great many things that enter into the cost of the product. It requires long experience and an intimate knowledge to enable a person to determine the question of actual cost, and to say whether the price is too great or otherwise. I would rather leave it to a general commission, something after the manner of the Railway Commission, which would be the proper method of dealing with the question, rather than that it should be left to people selected on any particular occasion when a charge happens to be made. I think a general commission would be much more effective, because, from the commencement, it would be gathering an amount of information which a commission appointed on the spur of the moment to deal with one particular case could not possibly obtain. The Railway Commission, from the commencement, have been gathering information in regard to all matters connected wdth railways. This information will be very valuable to have in our possession later on. The minister proposes, when the charge is made, to appoint somebody who has had no previous knowdedge of the matter-one to be appointed by the parties interested and one on the other side-and they would go into the question, but it does not seem to me that they would be abie to deal with it effectively.

As to not having persons of previous knowledge on the board that

it is intended to appoint, the representatives of the parties laying the complaint in all probability *would chose an expert, or a man who had a special knowledge of the conditions that they wished to inquire into, and in the same way the combine is likely to choose the man most familiar with its business. In that way you are sure of getting two men with a special knowledge of the things which are to be inquired into.

I presume that there would not be much difficulty from the standpoint of the combination, which, no doubt, would be. in a position to pick out a man from their own establishment who was familiar with the conditions of that establishment. But when the minister goes outside and looks for a man who has never been in the establishment, has no connection with it and could not possibly have an intimate knowledge of its affairs, I do not see how he would be in a position to get a suitable man for the other side. However, it is not my -intention at the present stage to say anything further in regard to the matter.

It must be generally admitted that the Bill introduced by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. King) will have a marked effect in correcting influences which we all feel are at work to-day. However, I believe that most of us recognize the fact that while the evils are a constant condition, the means that we are adopting will only be employed occasionally, and that if we can devise a measure which would be in continual operation on the evils of trust formation and at the same time not interfere with capital we would be taking a step in the right direction.
It has been said this afternoon that we should delay this matter for another year. I believe that the present is the most opportune time to act. We have at the present time, to be sure, a large number of pools and combines, but in so far as the more advanced forms of trusts are concerned they are not particularly numerous as yet. However, in the last few months we have had several in course of construction, and when we look back to the years 1898, 1899 and 1900 we will see an interesting condition of affairs. These were the years in which prosperity was returning to the United States, and these were the years in which trusts were most actively promoted. In this country at the present time we are at the threshold of an era of prosperity, and we may probably expect a number of trusts to be formed in practically all departments of manufacture in the next three or four years. For that reason, before we have vested interests and strong influences
to contend with, I think it would be opportune for us to adopt some - legislation which would control the matter of trust formation.
I may say that an examination of the conditions under which trusts are formed leads me to think that they have many economic advantages and that they may be of great benefit to the community at large. I wish, first, to run over shortly some of the minor benefits of trust formation. For instance, we have the concentration of office forces, the distribution of special processes and patents, the employment and specializing of the best talents, the very large element of saving in the matter of cross freights under agreements which may be made with the railways, alliances for banking with financial houses permitting them to secure better rates in respect of their_short loan, the reduction in the number of selling agents, reduction in the cost of advertising, self insurance, and advantages in securing raw materials, which we- see exemplified especially with respect to the United States steel corporation. Those that I have mentioned are simply the minor advantages of trust finance. Simply looking over these minor advantages, I think we see that the trust is of economic importance to the public. However, we have major advantages, and it is in connection w7ith these that we find most of the difficulties which are to be met by legislation. We have, for instance, the control which the trusts have over labour and labour organizations. An independent concern having its contracts to fill can be held up at almost any time by a labour organization, and will in the vast majority of cases be compelled to accede to its demands. In the case of a trust we have something entirely different, and as we know by the many instances which have occurred in the last ten years, labour unions and labour organizations can be fought by a trust when they could not be met by an independent operator in the same way. Another thing that we have is the control by the trusts of the jobbers, wholesalers and middlemen in general, and here, as has been said by several .speakers this afternoon, is where we find the process of compelling wholesalers to buy only from them and not deal with an independent manufacturer. The last and greatest benefit of the trust formation is the elimination of competition. That factor is one which will not be acknowledged, perhaps, by many of those representing the trusts, as the most important factor. In looking over the investigation of trusts by the United States government, and especially the investigation conducted by the Lexow Commission, you find that the officers of the trusts always quibbled upon this matter. But there happens to be abundant

evidence of it in connection with the prospectuses and formation of these trusts. I believe that trusts are of economic value, that they will be in ever increasing numbers amongst us, and that it is only going to be a comparatively short time when we will have a number of trusts formed in connection with practically all the staples in daily use.
That being the case it becomes a matter of importance for us to deal with measures such as that submitted by the Minister of Labour. I wish in the first place to speak for a moment, because it has a bearing on the rest of my argument, in regard to what I might call the assembling of trusts. We have first the promoter, who has perhaps the most important place in connection with trust finance. The promoter must send his experts to the different concerns that are intended to be taken into the trust; he must examine their finances, find out what their earning power is, estimate exactly what can be secured by an amalgamation of such interests. He must then present his case to the second factor who is what you might call the syndicate manager. It is from him that he must secure the necessary funds to get an option on the different properties. Consequently, we have here two factors, the syndicate managers and the promoters, who must be paid in the process of the trust formation. Now, the promoter having gone carefully over his ground and having secured his option, comes face to face with the question of capitalization, and I want to refer to that for a moment because it is of interest in connection with some of the more recent trusts that have been formed in Canada. The general procedure in the case of the trusts formed in the United States was this:	The earning power of
the independent concerns going into the trust was taken as a basis. This was capitalized and in most cases the capitalization of the actual earning power of the independent concerns was taken as the preferred stock of the trust. This was increased to a certain extent to allow for profits to the promoters and to the syndicate managers and underwriters. In the next place the assemblage of the independent concern was considered from this standpoint; that of the possibility of its earning power as a combine. All the factors of the elimination of competition and savings in other directions were taken into consideration, and these were capitalized. Usually it represented the common stock which in most instances was, roughly, equal to the preferred stock. In the case of a great many of the United States concerns the capitalization in the shape of preferred and common stock, was roughly perhaps a little more than double the value of the independent concerns on the basis of their replacement value. Now, that per-

haps looks conservative, but the course of subsequent events showed in almost every, case that the trusts of the United States were overcapitalized. But, while that was the case in the United States, I want to say that in Canada the formation of the trusts we have had recently has shown something in the shape of over capitalization very very much in excess of this. I will not venture to name all the combines, but some information has come into my hands in the last few months in regard to the capitalization represented by some of the Canadian trusts. There was one case of which I had some knowledge in which the whole concern could probably be replaced at a cost of $75,000. When this went into the trust the return was $200,000 in actual cash, and $250,000 in preferred and common stock. In another instance the replacement value of the concern entering the trust would probably be about $30,000. In that case the owner of that manufacturing concern received in cash $75,000, in common stock $65,000 and in preferred stock $150,000. One other instance I will mention, and this is in a different trust from the last I referred to, and it is this: The replacement value would perhaps be $750,000 and part of that was represented by a plant which was out of date and useless. However, the owners in that case received $598,000 in cash, $598,000 in bonds, $370,000 in preferred stock and $190,000 in common stock. I am just giving these illustrations to show that in the trust formation going on in Canada at present there is an immense overcapitalization. Perhaps some one will say:	That is of no interest to this
House; if people wish to overcapitalize their businesses they simply are not going to pay such large dividends. But I want to point out that there are some evils arising from this matter of overcapitalization. In the first place the overcapitalization of these stocks removes them from the realm of investment securities. Even in the more conservative capitalization of the United States trusts the preferred and common stock were never represented as investment securities; they were the speculative stocks, and this overcapitalization here as in the United States would throw upon the market a vast mass of speculative stock as distinguished from investment securities. This system had the element of danger that it floods the market with speculative stock of the industrials as they are called, and it has given rise to nine-tenths of the stock speculation.
I venture to say that there is more gambling in this form of stocks in one day on the stock exchanges than there is on all the Tace courses of Canada and the United States for a whole year. For that reason I say that this overcapitalization, simply from the fact that it gives birth to these

speculative stocks, is a matter of importance to us. In the next place the overcapitalizations is the means by which the savings of the man of small wealth are amalgamated into the pool of the trust. I took twenty-one of the representative trusts formed in the United States between 1898 and 1899, and I found that the prices at which these stocks were first sold upon the market and the prices in 1903-and here I might draw to your attention that the years from 1898 to 1903 were years of increasing prosperity-I found that the difference in the prices of these stocks between 1898 and 1903 represented a shrinkage of $400,000,000 in the case of the twenty-one trusts to which I refer. That simply meant one of the factors, and an important factor, by which 98 per cent of the wealth of the United States has filtered into the pockets of 55 per cent of the population. And I say, Sir, that for that reason overcapitalization in any of the corporations thus formed is an evil. In the next place, these companies attempt not to go back upon the glowing prospectuses which they issued to the public; they try to pay dividends upon their preferred and common stock where possible, and the result is that the money going to their reserve fund and their renewal fund kept on diminishing so that their overcapitalization really reacted upon the trusts with serious results. In the next place, the presence of this water in the stock blinds the public to the actual profits made by these corporations, If the people see that only 7 per cent is paid upon the stocks, they look upon it as a legitimate business operation, regardless of the fact that three-quarters of the entire stock probably represents water. For that reason, as soon as the trust finds that it is paying large dividends they cut a melon or in other words distribute among themselves a new issue of stock, and the public will continue to see only seven or eight per cent paid and are blinded to the actual condition of affairs. Another thing is that if these trusts and other companies were capitalized upon a more conservative basis, we would have a still greater increase in investment securities instead of the flooding of the market with speculative securities. There is one more lesson that was learned by this overcapitalization and it was this: That many of the panics and crises that have occurred in finance in the last few years have simply resulted from collapses of some of these speculative stocks due to overcapitalization. There is one other thing that is more important than any thing else in connection with the formation of trusts, and that is that the stocks get into the hands of the public with the result that many men who would perhaps give their support to legislation opposed to the trusts, simply because they
have this stock which they are afraid may drop in value, are converted into adherents of the trusts, Professor Mead, of the University of Pennsylvania, whose work on trusts and finance is perhaps better known than any other, and who cannot be said to be an opponent of trusts, uses these words:
Legislation or competition is always threatening the profits of the trusts. By enlisting a large number of investors in its support, the directors of the company may make valuable friends of the mammon of unrighteousness, who, when it fails, may fight manfully in its defence.
I merely mention the matter of capitalization because I feel that we should deal with that when we are dealing with the trust problem in a general way.
We have then the evils of the trust which we should consider most prominently. First, there is the control of labour, in regard to which the Lemieux Act is as useful as anything could be. In the next place, in regard to the control of middlemen and wholesalers, so far as it may injure independent men, I believe the present Bill of the Minister of Labour will be useful. We have, however, left, in a way that I do not think this Bill sufficiently meets, the question of over capitalization and the question of the enhancing of prices through the elimination of competition. I do not know that I should use the term enhancing prices, because I will admit that prices are not always increased by the combine. However, there is an enhancing of the margin between the cost of production and the selling price to the consumer, which amounts to the same thing. In regard to overcapitalization, I think we should have a provision in our law limiting the capitalization to the actual investment or to replacement values, plus, in the case of trusts, say 10 per cent for the services of the promotors underwriter syndicate manager.
May I ask the hon. gentleman how he would deal with the goodwill of a business?
The hon. member is a lawyer and is well versed in trust finance. He is probably well aware that that question of good-will has often been raised before. It was raised in Germany several years ago.
It is not a question of my raising. You speak of a replacement value, and I merely ask if you consider a good-will an asset. You apparently say you do not.	*

I am trying to answer the hon. gentleman. The German government limited the capital to the actual investment or the replacement value, disregarding the good-will, and found that law to operate successfully and well. They

went further and refused to allow industrial stocks to be placed on the market until one year after the industry was in actual operation. I have' not looked into that question perhaps as carefully as some lawyers in the House have.
I should think business men would look into the question of goodwill, seeing that thousands and hundreds of thousands of dollars have sometimes been spent in creating the good-will of a business.
That becomes a question of the assets of the trust when it is formed.
It is not a question of replacement, though.

As I was saying, not only has that operated successfully in Germany, but some trusts in the United States have been floated on that basis; and while some hon. gentlemen may think that is not a good basis, I may say that the Union Steel Company, the Cramp Shipbuilding Company, and the International Harvester Company were floated on that basis, and floated most successfully. With regard to enhancing the margin between the cost of production and the selling price, there is a decision of the Supreme Court of the United States to the effect that while the interest of the investing public should be considered, the interest of the public is of permanent importance. It has been suggested that we should have a commission similar to the Railway Commission. I think myself that something of that kind would be the most successful method of controlling this matter. I believe that everything in the nature of a pool or combine or trust should be compelled to secure incorporation so that it would come under the jurisdiction of such a commission. The next proposal I would make is this, that this commission should have power to limit the dividend upon stock of the company, fixed as I have previously indicated. They should have power to limit that dividend to a certain amount, and to allow a further amount for the surplus fund and the renewal fund, and profits in excess of that should be used for increased payment of wages and in reducing the price to the consumer. Some one will say that is a most radical proposal; but we have at the present time such a law in actual operation in this country, that is, in the city of Toronto. We have there a monopoly, just as one of these trusts is a monopoly, in the shape of the Consumers' Gas Company. That, I think, is on all-fours with the matter we have under discussion to-night. The dividends of the Consumers' Gas Company are limited to 10 per cent upon the capital; the amount to be placed in the reserve fund is fixed; in addition, there is 5 per cent allowed for Mr. M. CURRIE.
renewals. When the reserve fund reaches 50 per cent of the capitalization, all further profits are employed in reducing the price of gas to the consumers in Toronto. That has worked effectively in the city of Toronto, and while it may be a radical proposal, I feel like saying that what we need is a consumers' gas law enlarged and made applicable to the trusts in the Dominion of Canada.
