I am in receipt of many letters from parties who say that before this Bill is passed they ought to be given an opportunity to be heard, and I think that the best course would be to have it referred to a special committee which will hear the parties interested. Many of my correspondents complain that, under this Bill, any six persons, who may say that they are- of opinion that a combine exists, may, because they have had a dispute with some firm, compel that firm to subject its business to an investigation. For instance a jobber may get five of his clerks with himself to make a complaint, and put a merchant, against whom the jobber has a grudge, to a lot of expense, and compel him to make public to the committee all the details of his

business. If this Bill be proceeded with, : such a contingency ought to be avoided by i providing that the complaint should come j from six different houses in the same line ; of business. That is one of the complaints against this measure. These parties say that if it be referred to a committee they would gladly come before it and make such recommendations as they may deem necessary in order that we may have a perfect measure on our statutes.
That would shu* out the right of consumers to make complaint.
They would have the right to come before the committee and give evidence.

We have a Bill for the prevention of combines and suppression of combines formed in restraint of trade, which has been in force for some fourteen years, and under which the rights of the people have been reasonably protected. No complaint has come from the public so far as I can learn, but from some of the combines which consider they have been unjustly prosecuted. That law stands to-dav, and under it any man who feels he is aggrieved, and believes there is a combine in restraint of trade, can swear out information before a magistrate; and if a prima facie case be made out, it will go before a judge and jury in the ordinary course. This Bill is a very important measure. No doubt the public are entitled to be protected against monopolies and combines which are in restraint of trade and unduly enhance prices, but there are today very important considerations in this connection which we must not lose sight of. We in Canada are endeavouring to build up our trade in the best possible fashion, and our neighbours to the south are endeavouring to get control as much as possible of the markets of this country. Combines of necessity must arise in this country, hut not necessarily combines in restraint of trade, or in any way detrimental to consumers. It has been pointed out to-day that, in a majority of instances, the united capital and ability of combined companies are such that these combines can usually manufacture cheaper than could the isolated factories previously. I suppose there is no one in this country who would have any objection to a combine which reduced prices, or did not unduly enhance them. This Bill starts out by declaring that it is an Act to provide for an investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers, not which do enhance, but which may enhance prices, or may restrict competition to the detriment of the consumers. I do not think there is an hon. gentleman in this House who has any desire to prevent any business men of Canada combining in any lawful fashion
for the purpose of putting large masses of capital and skilled labour in the way of getting the very best results, provided the public are fairly treated. Yet this Bill starts out with the declaration that a combine of any kind, the result of which may be, if it choses to act unlawfully, to enhance prices, may be brought under its operation. I do not think that the hon. minister has any such intention. I think the Act should provide that only such combines as do enhance prices and restrict competition should be dealt with.

How does my hon. friend purpose to discover a combination of that kind until there has been some investigation, how will he be able to show that the combination comes under the class he is speaking of?

As I understand, six persons have to come forward to make a charge of that kind, because section 5 says: Where six or more persons are of opinion that a combine exists, and that prices have been enhanced. That is why I thought the body of the Act implied what I am arguing for, that you might have a perfectly fair, and reasonable combination that might reduce prices, and I did not think the minister had any objection to that. Section 5 indicates that that is the intention, but the minister starts with a heading which I do not think is justified. I merely raise the matter for consideration at 'this stage, because I feel that we have to give Canadian manufacturers as well as Canadian workingmen every reasonable chance for competition on fair grounds. We have a Tight to protect the public, and those engaged in manufacturing, and the idea is to put down monopolies that increase prices or unduly restrict competition.

In the province of Ontario there have been rather extreme cases of wrong and injustice, arising out of an attempt to prosecute men under the Combines Act; and as those men have been exposed to cost, and serious interference with their business, I think the House ought to he very careful before they go any further in this direction, without taking the utmost care not to repeat the absurdity that now exists. The whole question turns upon the one word : 'unduly.' The hon. gentleman has dwelt at length on that. There is no wrong in people combining to restrict production or l to enhance prices, the hon. gentleman ad, mits that, but it is wrong to unduly restrict , or unduly enhance. No merchant knows, no [DOT] manufacturer knows, as a fact, whether * what he is doing is undue or not. One man . may be of opinion that he is acting unduly, ' another man will say the very opposite, and E the law now requires a manufacturer or a i merchant to take his risk of being a crim-

inal. That is the position, that has been the position, and what the merchants, and others complain of is that if they come here to the Department of Trade and Commerce to ascertain whether what they propose to do is legal they cannot obtain any information. They may say that they find it absolutelv essential in the interest of trade to restrice production beyond a certain amount because if they flood the markets with ready-made clothing, for instance, they will cause injury to business and injury to the public interest. Perhaps half a dozen manufacturers of ready-made clothing meet, and come to the honest conclusion that there is danger of an excess of production in that line, doing no good to anybody, and that the output should be restricted to a certain amount. These gentlemen are confronted by this statute, and somebody says that "they must not do that unduly. I know that people in that position have come to Ottawa, and have naturally gone to the Department of Trade and Commerce to get some hint or indication of how far they might go, what would be considered reasonable, or when their conduct would be an undue restriction of trade or an undue enhancement of price. The Department of Trade and Commerce say that they cannot advise them, that they must take thee risk of doing this thing unduly or that they should go'do the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice says that it is a question of fact, and they must go to a jury to have a decision whether their action is reasonable or otherwise. Then these people, as respectable as any in the Dominion, wishing to keep within the law, knowing from their business knowledge and believing that what they do is right, and reasonable, proceed with what they have proposed. What is the result? Somebody takes it into his head that he can worry these men and knowing that it will not cost him one cent, that if he lays an information the government will have to bear the expense, and will conduct the prosecution in the name of the Crown, a prosecution is begun.
Is the hon. gentleman speaking of this measure or of the law as it stands?
The law as it stands.
The legislation enacted in 1899.

I do not want to have the minister perpetuate that injustice. A notorious case has occurred, the orosecu-tion of the Grocers' Guild. These people were charged with being a combine, and for three or four years they were held up to the people of this country as criminals. The outcome of that three years' prosecution was that the Chief Justice of Ontario Mr. BARKER.
held that they were within the law, that they had never exceeded the law in any sense, that their action did not come within the meaning of the word ' undue '; but these gentlemen only found that out after three or four years' litigation, costing them in round figures $12,000. The people who were prosecuting them were safe, the whole thing was done in the name of the King, and those who caused all that expense, trouble, annoyance and injury to the men concerned, got off scot free. The minister, before proceeding any further in experi ments on this law, should take the utmost care that he is right. I do not think the members of this House are the best people to judge exactly what the change should be. The minister may have considered it with great care, I presume he has, but I do not think that even the minister has the knowledge or the experience to judge how far he should go or how far this House should go in altering, this law. I have no doubt that some years ago when the House put in the word ' unduly ' they thought they were settling the whole thing. I hope we are not going to do any more blundering of that kind. I think that the proper course for the minister would be_ to refer this Bill to a special committee, who will give to all concerned an opportunity of coming before them and discussing these matters. We may then learn from experienced men who know all the difficulties and who can speak with knowdedge. We should not make another blundering attempt to deal with a subject of the utmost difficulty. We are now going^ to submit to arbitration the very question that, in the past, has been found so difficult to deal with under the present law. Some gentlemen who have considered the matter with a great deal of care, think there ought to be an opportunity given to them, through some department of the government, to know in advance whether what they are proposing to do is likely to make criminals of them or not. We have a Department of Trade and Commerce here, I do not know exactly how broad the functions of that department may be, but surely that department and not the De-parment of Labour should be the forum where questions relating to trade and commerce may be discussed. Now if we are going to spend large sums of money in this sort of arbitration-and as I understand the minister, the country is going to stand the shot on both sides, as a rule-we mivht better spend that money in enlarging, if need be, the scope of the Trade and Commerce Department, and keep these 'people out of crime rather than letting them into it, and then punishing them for it.

I want to add that in addition to the state of affairs which the

hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) pointed out continuing to exist, as it will, whether this law is passed or not, and, therefore, people will still be subject to prosecution as they have been in the last fourteen years, I want to point out that this Act goes beyond the criminal law in one most material respect. The criminal law under which prosecutions have heretofore been conducted, subclause (c), reads as follows:
Every person who conspires, combines, agrees or arranges with any other person, or with any railway, steamship, steamboat or transportation company ... to unduly prevent, limit or lessen the manufacture or production of any such article or commodity, or to unreasonably enhance the price thereof.
Is guilty of a misdemeanour. Now, the Minister of Labour leaves out the word ' unreasonably ' before the word ' enhance,' and that makes this new Act go beyond the criminal law, which has already given the business men of Canada enormous difficulty, and put them to enormous expense, men who are honestly desiring to live within the law. I know that business men have come to consult me, asking an explanation of the words 'unduly' and 'unreasonably', and I have told them that they would have to go before a judge and a jury to get an explanation. The law as it is now suggested reads: 'An Act to provide for the investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers which may enhance prices, not which unreasonably _ does enhance prices,' which would be in accord with the criminal law to-day. There is not a business man in this country who does not know' that there may be a dozen causes which make it perfectly proper for prices to advance in the future as there may be a dozen causes which may make it proper for prices to be reduced. But there was under the present Act the possibility that prices might be enhanced reasonably and yet that would be an offence. This Bill says that when six men are _ of opinion that something of this kind is occurring, they may actually put the business men of the country to the expense of having this investigation. But that it is not the worst part of it. Anybody who has had anything to do with these prosecutions knows that everybody attacked has got to produce all his books, ledgers, letter books, invoices and other documents by the hundreds or thousands, that the whole of his business is turned upside down, that the books w'anted in daily use are one time in the court and at another time somewhere else, instead of being in his office. He is put to all kinds of inconvenience and expense other than mere legal expense, when he is trying to act in good faith, and this Bill actually
goes beyond even the criminal law o! to-day and makes it worse for the business men of Canada than it was before.

It appears to me the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Bristol) somewhat misconstrues the true meaning of this Act. As I understand it, the Act substitutes a board of arbitration for criminal proceedings before a judge and jury.

It does not do it, for obvious reasons. First of all, the criminal law is not repealed, it is nnnply enforced, and anybody can start a prosecution. Secondly, I quoted the criminal law, and I have shown that the word 'unreasonably' is left out before the word 'enhanced' in the new7 Bill.

I agree that that portion of the Criminal Code is not repealed, but instead of substituting I might say it amplifies the proceedings under the Criminal Code by giving the right of arbitration, which seems to me a milder procedure than taking proceedings under the Criminal Code.
Anybody can still lay an information.

They can if they choose. But to take proceedings under the Criminal Code you are immediately up against all the legal technicalities that can be raised; whereas a board of arbitrators is more inquisitorial than judicial. The board of arbitrators can go into the matter on equitable grounds, they can make a broader inquiry than could be done in proceedings under the Criminal Code. Any six men can lay information and make a complaint, then the arbitrators are chosen, one for each side, and a third is selected by the tw'O. The men complained against are not supposed to be criminal. Then if the board of arbitrators find that they are unduly and improperly, by their combination, enhancing prices or restricting trade to the detriment of the public, they then make their report. If, after the report is published in the 'Canada Gazette', these people continue to violate the spirit of the law, then they are subject to a penalty of $1,000. It seems to me this Act is quite an improvement on the Criminal Code. The Criminal Code will not be invoked if this Act comes into force, and you will have more ample justice done in all such cases than you will have under proceedings under the Criminal Code, which are expensive and liable to all sorts of legal technicalities. These proceedings will be inexpensive, thev will reach the end of justice more speedily and more equitably than any law at present on the statute-book.
Evidently the House is of opinion that this Bill removes those clauses which 'provide for prosecution under the Criminal Code.
No.

Then, we will assume the position to be as it actually is. This law provides a convenient form of investigation into the affairs of a business concern, in other words, it is an inquest. It is suspected that there may be a combination, not that there is a combination, but that there may be. Immediately an investigation is set on foot, and provision is made under this Act whereby there are arbitrators appointed, who are to hear all this evidence without being under the rules of evidence, they are not governed by the rules of evidence.
Certainly they are governed by the rules of evidence.

You will find they are not. They are in a similar position to the Railway Commission, and they will not he governed by the rules of evidence. They will conduct their investigation in their own way, and they will have the power to go into the business of everybody and into everybody's books. When their finding is published in the ' Canada Gazette ' anybody can carry on a criminal prosecution, and he will have all the evidence that has been taken, by this investigating committee-this detective committee-to make a criminal out of the man who has been investigated. I think in justice to the business interests of the country, the minister should send this Bill to a committee, and those people who are crying out so loudly and writing those articles in the paper should be asked to come and substantiate their charges. I do not think there are very many combines in this country. There is every reason why we should not go beyond the straight, fair way of dealing as between man and man and as between man and the law. A man should not be found guilty before he is tried. In an ordinary criminal case, if a detective acts in this manner and gives a man, charged with a criminal offence, what is known as the third degree, the jury dismisses the case and there is a mistrial. I do not think the minister realizes how far reaching this Bill is, and I think that in justice to the business interests and to all interests involved, it should be referred to a committee so that we might have an opportunity of hearing about these combines. There is no evidence of a satisfactory character to show that there are any combines or that combines are unduly enhancing prices. I understood that an arrangement had been made between the whips whereby this Bill should be referred to a special committee.
There was no such arrangement made.
The chief whip told me there was such an arrangement.
There was not.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: There never was such an arrangement made.
The hon. gentleman might possibly have misunderstood.

The minister is putting himself up as the chief trust buster of this country. They have had trust busters in the United States, but men who go about trust busting do not happen to travel very long in public life. I think that in justice to both sides concerned, the consumers who are ground down, according to their lights, and also the manufacturers and business interests, which are liable to be. prosecuted under this Bill, should be heard before any action is taken. I think we may be able then to get a Bill that will reach this difficulty. Supposing that this Bill gives the right, which has not been given in any British country, to lay a charge and investigate any man's business, persons may take advantage of it for political or religious reasons, or they may do it out of mere spite, because there are men who are so mean that they do not wish to see their fellow men succeed in making a little money. They may do a man an enormous amount of injury, they may ruin him, because if they start an investigation the banks will refuse him credit. There are legal gentlemen on the other side of the House who will appreciate the situation. Is a man going to be considered a criminal, is he going to be investigated in reference to his conduct, character and business relations under this Bill? This commission may free him but that does not mean that some enemy of his cannot level a prosecution against him under the Criminal Code. You must amend the Code if you are going to put this Bill into force. Two clubs are two too many. For that reaston I make the suggestion that all parties be heard before a commitee of the House.
I do not think the Bill will have the effect that the hon. gentleman has stated. It seems to be a more moderate means of investigating such questions.
But there is the Criminal Code, and it does not take the place at all of the previous Act.

Admitting that criminal proceedings may still be taken, it is not reasonable to assume that both lines of action would be taken. A person would be far more likely to take action under this Bill, because he would not be required to

accuse the other party of any criminal conduct. It is a mere investigation, and there is the safeguard. It takes six persons to secure this investigation. One may make a complaint under the Criminal Code. Then, there is the further safeguard that a complaint is made to a judge of the High Court and he may refuse the investigation. He may not find sufficient grounds. That means that a man's business is not wantonly dragged into the daylight. But, if he does find sufficient ground the investigation has to go on, then who is appointed to hold the investigation. One is appointed as the representative of the parties making the complaint and the other is nominated by the party accused. If they cannot agree, a third is appointed by the minister. What happens if there is an investigation? As far as I have gone into the Bill, I must say that I approve of it.
I think it is a timely measure, and I am not going to worry myself very much as to whether they have such a measure somewhere else or not. It looks to me to be a good measure for Canada, and if so, it is sufficient for my purpose. Subsection 2 of section 18 reads as follows:
In deciding any question that may affect the scope or extent of the investigation, the board shall consider what is required to make the investigation as thorough and complete as the public interest demands.
I submit that is one great step in advance. Then, the following section provides for publicity and if there is anything that will tend to give the consumers fair play it is the fact that the light of day may be let in on the whole transaction by a board whose only object is to see justice done in the public interest. It is generally assumed and I believe it to be true that there are in existence combines which injuriously affect the public, and enhance the price of commodities that are used generally by the people.
What about dredging?

My honoured friend has something on his brain, and he very often tries to enlighten the House, but he seems to have so much mud about it that no one understands it except himself. I am not discussing this frivolously. So far as I have looked into the Bill it contains a great deal of good, and I would judge that my hon. friend the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Bristol) does not understand the Bill as I understand it. It seems to me that having regard to the legal capabilities of the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Bristol) he ought to be able to see good and not evil in this Bill. I confess that" before I read the Bill, taking only the comments in the press, I had not a very high opinion of it, but since I have gone over its
provisions, I am quite in sympathy with it, and for my part I should like to see it become law.

I have studied the Bill, and I have listened carefully to the lengthy speech of the junior minister. His verbosity was such that I really could not understand what he meant, and I doubt very much if he understood himself. He referred to the fact that the father of my seat mate had gone into the matter so thoroughly in 1888 that this Minister of Labour thinks to-day that the evidence then collated was sufficient to induce any government to take steps to protect the public. The minister used that as an argument against the Conservative administration, but I would point out that for the fourteen years this government has been in power, day after day, and month after month, and year after year they saw that combines were being formed against the public interest: lumber combines, cement combines, machinery combines, meat combines, all calculated to plunder the public, and the government during these long years never raised a hand to protect the people. Well* the only excuse for the minister's argument is his youth. During fourteen years this government has never done a single act to protect the farmers of the west from being eaten up body and soul by these combines, their farms mortgaged, their children half naked in some instances. At last, this gracious government, and its Minister of Labour has awakened from their Rip Van Winkle sleep, and so they now propose to do something. In 1888, Mr. Clarke Wallace brought out the fact, that there were thirteen combines in Canada that needed to be combatted, but the Minister of Labour is a member of a government that has created a fish combine, one of the worst combines that has cursed the west. It was his government that gave the people up in the northwestern part of my riding, a monopoly of the fisheries for a mere trifle, and which for a mere song, threw away to a few grafters and party heelers the heritage eff the people of that western country. I say grafters, and I mean every word of it. Suppose the Minister of Labour does not know about that just as he knows very little about any subject that I have heard him discuss in this House. This government, of which he is a member, gave to Coffey and Merritt, the fishing in Cedar lake, 285 square miles of the finest fisheries in the west; they gave away in Moose lake 522 square miles of sturgeon fishing; in Cormorant lake 140 square miles; in Cumberland lake 166 square miles, in Amiak lake 90 square miles, in Namea lake 66 square miles, a total of 1,300 square miles for the paltry sum of I $300 per annum. To these people this

government gave a fishing monopoly, which is absolutely another word for a combine. And the result is that the gentlemen who got that monopoly from this government sold that monopoly to an American fish firm. The winter season is the only season of the year that fishermen have a chance to be independent, and to sell their product in the highest market, but these poor fishermen, under an agreement made with this government, were compelled to sell their products to this Northwest Fish Company of Americans for from one cent to one-and-three-quarter cents per pound less than they could get in the open market. It was the officials of this government who compelled the poor fishermen to do that. In the winter of 1907-8, the fishermen were compelled to sell their product at less than market prices all through the winter, and in the spring of 1908 the company went into liquidation and became bankrupt. I read affidavits last yeai', and I am going to read them now, from men who produced the fish sold to the company, compelled to be sold to this American company by the officials of this government, who have awakened to the fact that they had to protect the people at this late day. These fishermen had to sell at less than market prices, and when this American company went into liquidation, they could not get even the poor recompense that they were compelled to accept for their output. I will now quote an affidavit which I read last year:
This is to certify that I, Isaac Bradbury, fished during the winter of 1907-08 in the waters covered by Capt. E. D. Coffey and F. L. Merritt's leases in the Northwest Territories, and was forced to sell my catch by the government officials to the Northwest Fish Company, which is represented by Capt. E. D. Coffey and F. L. Merritt, and that the Northwest Fish Company went into bankruptcy and owe me $810 for my winter's labour.
This affidavit is declared before George O. Bellamy, and is signed by Isaac Bradbury, fisherman. I brought this matter up last year before the Minister of Fisheries, who promised me explicitly in this House that he would have his commissioners inquire into this matter and protect the producers; but no effort has been made to protect my friend Mr. Bradbury, and other men who are in the same position. I had another letter from Mr. Bradbury the other day. He states that he had a letter from me saying that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was going to investigate the matter, and he goes on to say:
I think he should, for the government gave that Northwest Fish Company the privilege of getting the fish out of those lakes for practically nothing, and now the property that we, the creditors, have to fall back npon to get paid for our fish is worth Mr. CAMPBELL.
nothing, for the lakes are pretty nearly cleaned out, and it is no good for any company to buy. I think the government should consider me and the other creditors the way that we have been used. It would have been bad enough if the Northwest Fish Company had paid the $80 per ton. That was u.. price they were to pay, hut at the same time the Armstrong Fish Company were prepared to pay $110 per ton for the same fish, hut we could not sell to them, for the government officials would not allow us. We were forced to give them to the Northwest Fish Company, which was pretty hard on me, for I had to hire my men, and what little money I did not earn I had to pay out. The hardship of fishing is very great, and I think this is a case where the government has a right to protect the poor producers as against the company that holds the fishing under a special license.
I am quoting that for tlie reason that this was a monopoly created by this government for the benefit of an American organization as against Canadians, and through it the resources of Canada were dissipated in a wrongful manner. It seems to me absolutely hypocritical for any member of a government to get up and make a speech such as was made here to-day by the Minister of Labour. The government cry anti-monopoly while they grant such monopolies as this. I was very much pleased to hear my hon. friend from Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) tell the House, and I am sure the House appreciated his remarks at their full value, that since he had been in public life he had been out for fair play to the public. I have put a very different interpretation upon his actions since I have known him. I may be wrong in some cases, but in this case I think I am not wrong in my interpretation, but he is wrong in his. That is all I want to say at present except that I agree with the proposition of my hon. friend from Simcoe that this matter ought to be put into the hands of a committee to investigate it most thoroughly. We know all the facts. All we want is the evidence, and when we get that, we want to send the perpetrators of harm to the place where they belong, and that is the penitentiary.

I have learned within the last few minutes that it is wrong to be young. I think the hon. minister's most bitter enemy must acknowledge that he has introduced and placed before the House this measure in a most capable manner. We are now, I understand, considering clause 1, and I think we should consider the various clauses of the Bill as we come to them. There are some amendments which I would like to see made to the Bill as proposed. I agree with the principle of the Bill, and I would like to see it advanced by considering the different clauses, and amending them if necessary as we come to them. I am quite sure that the hon. min-

ister wants only what is right, and is perfectly willing to insert in the Bill any amendment which will make a better Bill. I quite agree with my hon. friend from Toronto that the word may in the preamble is too wide, but I do not think we are now considering the preamble. If we are considering the preamble, this is the proper time to consider its wording, but if we are considering clause 1, I do not see any reason why we should not go on with its consideration, and not with that of the preamble.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Clause 1 is the clause before the committee.

Any one who looks at this Bill closely from a legal standpoint and endeavours to ascertain the ultimate effect it is likely to have, can imagine many difficulties which should demand from this committee the closest deliberation. There is a popular idea that anything devised under the name of a combine should be . condemned and blotted out of existence by legislation. I was unable to have the opportunity of hearing all the discussion, and, therefore, speak with the disadvantage which always comes from . that circumstance; but on examining this Bill with some little care, I realize that, so far as the definition of a combine contained in it is concerned, a combine in an illegal sense-because that I assume is what is intended by the definition-would, under its wording, cover every kind of organization, whether legal or illegal, in the sense in which we understood a combine in the past as a matter of law. The common law of England always applied only to such combines the effect of which would be the unreasonable enhancing of prices and bringing about a condition which ought not to exist.

Does my hon. friend observe also that, in considering clause (e), what I was pointing out is true, namely, that clause (c) gives an interpretation to a combine beyond what the criminal law does, and I do not suppose the hon. minister wants to go beyond the present law.

I was endeavouring to point out that a combine, as defined in this Bill, includes not merely those combines which are in the restraint of trade and which, in the past, were regarded by statute as well as by common law as illegal, but also those which in the past were always regarded as proper.
Quite so.

In that sense the definition is a very wide one, and I apprehend that the difficulties which may arise from the passage of this Bill may be
very great indeed, and ought to demand the closest deliberation and care from both sides of the House, irrespective of party.
In order to show that we ought not to legislate so as to declare that understandings or associations of business men, which may be called combines, are necessarily of such a character that they should come under the ban of the law or' legislation regarding combines, I would draw the attention of the committee to the condition of affairs which exists in England with regard to the various trade associations there, and which have existed right along. Some hon. gentlemen say that these combines only arise in countries where you have a protective tariff, but that these combines are to be found in England and are recognized and approved there is evidence that they are not exclusively due to that cause. Thus in March, 1908, no less a number than sixteen firms of spinners and fifteen firms of doublers in the spinning trade of Lancashire combined together. Their avowed object was not to create a monopoly, but by the centralization of office work and buying, selling and distributing arrangements, to lead to considerable economy. In addition to this, important benefits were expected to arise from an organization which would gradually provide that each mill should spin and double only those numbers and qualities to which its machinery is best adapted. Another advantage was expected to accrue from the application to each individual concern of the combined practical experience of the whole of the board of directors, exclusively composed of experts in that branch of business.
It is stated in this book from which I quote, which is entitled 'Trusts and the State,' and which is one of the Fabian essays, considered authorities upon this sub- ' ject, that these arrangements of trade are considered eminently proper. Some of the advantages are set forth in this work which flow from the association in business of people who are experts in the various branches. Take another industry, one which exists in a large degree in my own province. I refer to the coal mining industry. This book says:
The great foundational industry of coal mining might be expected to offer special facilities for combination of interests, as it is strictly limited in extent.
It refers to the combine arranged by Sir Geo. Elliot, a leading spirit in coal mining in England, and proceeds to say:
After setting forth the disadvantages under which individual lessees at present labour- the necessity of leaving boundary walls of coal unworked, the unnecessary increase in the expense of pumping, ventilation, and underground haulage, -which have to be treated, not in the most convenient manner, but according to the arbitrary divisions of

'ownership-Sir Geo. Elliot said:	' Briefly,
the efiect of amalgamation, it is contended, would be to remove all the artificial factors which now stand for so much in the sum of the coal mining industry and to leave science and nature face to face. The different coal districts would then be treated each as a whole, according to its geographical peculiarities. Under a more fully organized method of working, the whole of the coal) good and bad, could be systematically extracted, instead of being as now largely wasted for the sake of bringing up only those kinds which produce the highest market prices.	.
I could read various other extracts which go to show that these arrangements have worked beneficially and that the combines were eminently proper and ought not to be condemned by legislation. I have in mind a condition which exists in my, own county, where we have two coal mines in the one community working side by side. One of them works actually under such conditions that it is impossible for it to exploit a large quantity of its area. The adjoining company, which is separated from the first one by a barrier which has to be left, under the laws of the province, could advantageously work out this coal which is lost to the first. Would It be said that it would be improper for those two companies to combine and mine that large quantity of coal which, on account of the division of ownership, it is impossible for either to obtain.
When we are approaching the question as to what should be done regarding combines recognized as improper we should not throw into the pot these organizations which are proper and put them to the peril and risk of an extensive investigation that may be imposed on them under this Bill, or any peril to which only improper combines should be subjected. The effects of this Bill would be, to my mind, to create conditions under which a proper combine would be attacked just the same as the others. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Bristol) has pointed out that the effect of legislation in the past has been to make a combine a crime where it caused an unreasonable enhancement of prices or an undue limitation of competition. If you look at section 496 of the Criminal Code you will find that a conspiracy in restraint of trade is an agreement between two or more persons to do or procure to be done any unlawful act in restraint of trade.
So far we have only put under the ban those combinations and arrangements where the agreements between the two parties is to do the unlawful act. Then we make unlawful the combination of people whose object it is to unduly or to unreasonably enhance the price of goods. You must have the undue result, the unlawfuj result, or you must have the unlawful act. That is the position of the law to-day.

That is all right, those are combinations that ought to be attacked and prevented. If you have a combination of men in any business who combine together with the avowed object of increasing the price of any of the articles of necessity in life, that is an agreement against the state and the state should deal with it accordingly; but where, on the other hand, you have combinations such as I have indicated, existing in the various trades in England and in Canada, for their common interests, or for the purpose of saving fixed charges which are always an important consideration in manufacturing, for the purpose of obtaining the advantage of the knowledge and experience of men interested in trade together, there is a very marked line of divergence and that line should be maintained; we should hesitate before combining these two things together and dealing with them on the same basis. Of course one approaches the consideration of a measure prepared with great care by the minister, as I am sure this has been, and sympathetically view it as intended for the purpose of remedying some alleged evils, but when I find the section defining a combine as an agreement which has or is designed to have the effect of increasing or fixing the price-not unduly increasing it but merely fixing the price-I say we are passing from the realm of legislation where we have dealt with this thing in the past or where it has been dealt with under our. jurisdiction here and elsewhere, and coming into a new realm. I say it is not, as I have been able to read the cases or study the conditions, an improper thing for men interested in the same business to agree together about increasing prices, if they do not do it unduly. Suppose there are competitive trade conditions in this and several other countries and you have an industry which has been for a long time lagging indifferently as the result of competition with the United States and the price of the commodity goes up all over the world, the labouring men working in that industry have perhaps been struggling along at low wages because they have been unable to get as full return for their work in that industry as their brethren in some industry alongside; do you mean to say it is improper for the people interested in that trade to increase the price because the price of that commodity has gone up all over the world and let the men work in the industry have the result of that increase? I say I do not so regard it. It may be that there are some other sides to this matter, and I am approaching the consideration of it with the greatest care with the desire to arrive at a solution, but it does not seem to me we should create the position of penalizing a condition ol that kind. When you call a combine an agreement among business men to fix the

price, when it is not done unduly or unreasonably, you are rendering the problem as to whether you should deal with this matter somewhat more difficult. This section of the Bill speaks of an arrangement for an agreement which is to have the effect of increasing or fixing the price. Within what area in this Dominion are you going to fix the limits within which the understanding between the parties as to price is to be determined? For instance, if certain gentlemen in the province of Ontario engaged in the manufacture of some particular article peculiar to this province, agree to fix the selling price, how are you going to arrive at a decision _whether or not that is a price which is improper or which ought to be increased? It may be a price which even at the increased figure is less than that which is sought by some gentlemen engaged in the same business in another province in the Dominion under more advantageous circumstances.

They could not even lower the price.
. Mr. MACQONALD. Yes, my hon. friend is right, under this language you could not lower the price.
Does not the hon. gentleman see that the whole gist of the Act is that this must be to the detriment of the consumers? Clause 5 clearly says it is to the detriment of the public.

My hon. friend has read something with which I propose to deal in a moment. I am now pointing out that the definition of the word ' combine ' means the legislative ban being put upon certain understandings and arrangements which are included in the definition of that word and I object to that.
The words 'to the detriment of the public ' are nowhere contained in the definition with which my hon. friend is dealing.

I know that. At the conclusion of that section we also find that another legislative ban is being placed on a proposition that in the past has always been regarded as an eminently fair and reasonable one. After dealing "with various things, it says that this includes:
. Tlie acquisition, leasing or otherwise taking over, or obtaining by any person to the end aforesaid, of any control over or interest in the business, or any portion of the business, of any other person.
The result is that if a man has been eminently successful in the prosecution of an industry and he and his business associates have made money, and there is perhaps in the next county or province, another concern engaged in the same trade which is not so prosperous, then under this Bill 220
it is impossible for the prosperous and successful man to obtain any interest in the other business, and there is no opportunity for the successful man to expand. Supposing the other situation affords very great facilities for manufacturing, but that there have been some conditions which always may arise in business, through incompetency or otherwise, which prevent the second man from succeeding, then you do not permit the first successful man to obtain an interest in the other business with a view to resuscitating it, extending it or making it a success. It is true the words are limited by the words ' to the end aforesaid.' But if the result of the combination is that you are going to have joint control, of course there can only be one end of it, and that would be that the price between those two friendly concerns would be fixed. I think this is a proposition that ought to be carefully considered, because unless you do that you will impair the capacity to obtain capital in this country. If we do not preserve the safeguards for proper business arrangements, the opportunity to obtain capital will be impaired and after all, while we have had filtered into Canada, as you have seen it in the United States in the yellow press, a lot of talk about trusts, monopolies, and all that sort of thing, we sometimes forget, because we are alongside this great country with 80,000,000 people that we are only at "the threshold of our career, that we have only 8,000,000 people here, that we have not begun to develop our resources, and that what we want, above everything else, is to encourage the infusion of capital into Canada. What we want in this country is to encourage capital to come in, and ensure that it shall have safe returns, and that capitalists shall not be attacked improperly or illegitimately by legislation. Unless we do that I do not know where we are going to land in Canada. What we want to do is to legislate against those combines which unreasonably affect or unduly dislocate the business conditions of the country. My hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) says that no proceedings will take place unless prices have been enhanced, or unless you have some bad result from the combination. Now my hon. friend is a lawyer of great ability, he knows that a judge under this Act is not even called upon to ask that a prima facie case shall be made out. A prima facie case, I understand, is one upon which a judicial tribunal would be bound to decide in favour of the party making it unless it is answered in some way. The way in which these proceedings are taken is that a party files a statement alleging certain things. He does not need to give any grounds for his belief, but he merely files the usual declaration that to the best of his knoivledge and belief certain conditions exist. Then he goes before the judge, and

692i>
if tlie judge is satisfied not that a prima facie case is made out, but that there is reasonable ground for believing a combination exists-
Is that not a prima facie case?
No, reasonable grounds simply means that there is a plausible case made out which might be inquired into.
And that it is in the public interest that an -investigation shall be held.

That is where I find a difficulty with the minister's definition of a combine. The judge will look to see what is the public interest, and he will find that the public interest means anything contrary to what is mentioned as coming under the definition of the word 'combine'.
